title: Pénétrable de Chicago
medium: Plastic filaments and metal hanging hardware
altText: A large walk-in artwork made of countless thin plastic filaments hanging from a metal framework in a room, forming a dense curtain-like space that visitors can move through. The exact color and arrangement of the filaments have not been confirmed from the museum record.

context: Made in 1971 by the Venezuelan artist Jesús Rafael Soto, who was a leading figure in kinetic art, art that seems to move or vibrate. The Art Institute lists the medium as plastic filaments and metal hanging hardware, gives the size as about 3.2 by 5 by 9 meters, and tags it as an immersive environment.

descriptions.k: Imagine a room full of hanging strings that you can walk through! Jesús Rafael Soto made this. It has thousands of thin plastic threads. How would it feel to brush through them? What would you see as they sway?
descriptions.g12: Jesús Rafael Soto, an artist from Venezuela, made this artwork from thousands of thin plastic strings hanging from the ceiling. It is called a Pénétrable, which means you can go inside it and walk through. The strings move and shimmer as you pass. How would it feel to be inside an artwork instead of looking at one?
descriptions.g35: Jesús Rafael Soto was born in Venezuela and became famous for art that seems to move and vibrate. Pénétrable de Chicago is a huge environment about 5 meters wide and 9 meters long, made from plastic filaments hanging from metal hardware. The museum calls it immersive, and its title suggests you can enter it. How is walking through an artwork different from looking at a painting on a wall?
descriptions.g68: Soto, from Venezuela, worked in kinetic art, which creates the feeling of movement through vision or through real motion. In Pénétrable de Chicago (1971), thousands of plastic filaments hang in a space about three meters high, five meters wide, and nine meters long. The title means penetrable, and the museum calls it an immersive environment. How does an artwork that you can move through change the role of the viewer?
descriptions.g910: Soto's Pénétrables transform the viewer from observer into participant. Pénétrable de Chicago fills a room with plastic filaments hung from metal hardware, creating a space that surrounds the body, with dimensions of about 3.2 by 5 by 9 meters. The Art Institute classes it as an immersive environment. The effect of so many fine lines is likely to be optical vibration and a shifting sense of space, though the museum offers no description. Consider how participation changes meaning.
descriptions.g1112: Soto's work extends the optical experiments of kinetic art into physical space, asking viewers to enter the artwork instead of facing it. Pénétrable de Chicago, made of plastic filaments and hanging hardware, is documented by the Art Institute as an immersive environment but not described further, so claims about its effect are inferences from the medium and the genre. Interpretations might emphasize perception and vibration, the dissolving of the object, or the artwork as an experience shared with others. Each depends on how the work behaves when people actually move through it.

teacherNote.context: A 1971 walk-in environment by the Venezuelan kinetic artist Jesús Rafael Soto. The museum record gives materials, size and subject terms but no description, so this entry is cautious. The work is in copyright, so no image is linked yet.
directions: Hang strips of plastic or string from a doorway frame and let students walk through, then write or draw what they saw and felt.
Discuss why museums usually ask visitors not to touch art and what changes when an artist invites touch.
Compare an artwork you walk through with a painting you look at from a distance.
